en.title: How a computer works: from data to program
en.excerpt: From bits to instructions: what really happens between the keyboard and the result on screen.

tasks.title: Task 1: Lesson — from data to program
tasks.content:
A computer understands nothing: it executes instructions, in order, at absurd speed and without ever getting tired. Everything else is organisation.

The path of a program, in four layers:

  1. Data: everything is a binary number. A character is a number, an image is a table of numbers, a sound is a series of samples. The only unit the machine knows is the bit.
  2. Memory: a long sequence of numbered bytes. Every slot has an address. A variable is a name given to an address: the program handles names, the machine handles addresses.
  3. The instruction: an elementary operation (load, add, store, jump). A program is a long sequence of those.
  4. The cycle: the processor fetches the instruction at the address held in the program counter, executes it, moves on to the next. Nothing else. This is exactly where security starts: who controls the program counter, and what happens when you make it jump somewhere else?

Then comes the idea of a high-level language: you write x = 5 + 3, the compiler turns it into instructions, the assembler turns those into machine code, and the processor executes them. Every layer adds comfort… and sometimes bugs: buffer overflows exist precisely because the C layer does not protect memory.

Remember: a computer is an instruction machine that manipulates addresses. All security rests on controlling three things: the data, the addresses, and the program counter.

tasks.title: Task 2: Practice
tasks.content: Two questions: what the machine actually does, and what the language hides.

questions.question: What does a processor actually do?
questions.hint: The processor knows neither meaning nor intent: it follows a counter.
questions.explanation: The processor executes a stream of instructions driven by a program counter. Security of systems rests on controlling that counter — which is why defences such as the stack canary or NX exist.

questions.question: Why is C described as “close to the machine”?
questions.hint: It is not about speed, it is about guarantees.
questions.explanation: In C, memory management is the programmer's job: that is power (performance, control) and risk (overflows, use-after-free). It is exactly what the pwn.college labs exploit.

tasks.title: Task 3: Mission — the machine diagram
tasks.content:
In the lecture room, the Stanford course left its machine diagram (the document describing the layers, from data to processor).

Mission. Read that diagram and find the number of bytes given to one address (the address_size field).

questions.question: Find the address size (address_size, in bytes) given in the machine diagram.
questions.explanation: The size of an address sets the addressable memory space (2^64 bytes on 64 bits). It is also what makes addresses predictable without ASLR, hence the importance of randomisation.

tasks.title: Task 4: End-of-room exam
tasks.content: Four timed questions. 60% is enough to pass.

questions.question: What is a memory address?
questions.hint: It is what lets you reach one slot unambiguously.
questions.explanation: An address is the access number of a memory slot. A variable name is only a translation made by the compiler: at machine level there are only numbers.

questions.question: What is the program counter?
questions.hint: It decides where the program goes next.
questions.explanation: The program counter holds the next instruction. It is incremented after each instruction unless a jump changes it: hence the importance of the return address on the stack.

questions.question: What happens when a program is compiled?
questions.hint: The compiler produces another form of the program.
questions.explanation: Compilation chain: source → machine code → execution. The optimiser works on intermediate code, not on algorithms: the semantics must stay the same.

questions.question: Why does a garbage collector make exploitation harder?
questions.hint: The trouble with manual memory management is that it gets it wrong.
questions.explanation: In C the programmer frees memory: a double free or a use-after-free is a classic exploitable flaw. Automatic garbage collection removes that whole family of bugs — the argument behind memory-safe languages, which course 6.858 mentions at the end.
